plan.topic: Protein on tirzepatide: how much protein adults losing weight are generally advised to eat, why it matters when appetite drops (keeping lean mass), and practical ways to hit it with smaller meals
plan.angle:
Keep the title 'Protein on Tirzepatide: How Much and Why', the lane A label, the structure and all the safety lines. Make these changes:

(a) New opening: 'You're eating much less on tirzepatide, so is protein the thing to protect? Yes. The general adult baseline is zero point eight grams per kilogram of body weight a day, and a 2025 advisory from four nutrition and obesity groups suggests eating your protein food first at meals so you're more likely to get enough.' Don't say 'every meal'.

(b) Chapter 2: give the RDA of 0.8 g/kg/day (US National Academies, also quoted in the advisory). Show the kg and lb working, using whole numbers and a sentence of its own for each decimal. Optionally add: 'For people actively losing weight, higher targets of about 1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram have been proposed, and experts don't yet agree on which body weight to use, because using your actual weight can overestimate what you need. One practical range they mention is 80 to 120 grams a day.' Attribute it to the 2025 ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS advisory. Never say 'you should eat X g' and never say 'recommended for tirzepatide users'. Add: 'Very high intakes, around 2 grams per kilogram or more for a long time, aren't advised. A registered dietitian can set your number.'

(c) Chapter 3: 'protein first' is the advisory's suggestion. Call it 'recommended', never 'proven on tirzepatide'.

(d) Chapter 5: food first. Then: 'The advisory says shakes, bars and fortified foods can help some people reach their protein target.' Replace the 'not shown to protect muscle' line with: 'There's no product the advisory recommends for protecting muscle. Protein plus strength training is the combination it highlights.' No brand names or product shots.

(e) GI line, credited to the advisory: 'Nausea, diarrhoea and constipation are common. Smaller, more frequent meals and avoiding fatty foods, especially early on, can help.' 'Eating slowly' may stay as our own tip with no source tag.

(f) Chapter 6: quote the advisory's point that protein alone is likely not enough to keep muscle without strength training, then give 2 or more days a week of muscle-strengthening (WHO / US Physical Activity Guidelines), started gently.

(g) Chapter 7, check with a clinician first: kidney disease or risk of it, being told to limit protein or fluids, pregnancy, and anyone with a history of disordered eating, who should set targets with their care team rather than track numbers. Keep 'consider asking for a registered dietitian referral'.

(h) Thanksgiving plate: frame it as 'build the plate around turkey or another protein you enjoy, then whatever else you like'. No guilt, no 'earn it', no foods labelled bad, no calorie talk.

(i) DXA chapter: as written (160 scanned; 124 on tirzepatide, all doses pooled, vs 36 on placebo; 72 weeks; no diabetes; about 75% fat / about 25% lean; lean mass isn't pure muscle).

No drug dose numbers anywhere. Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' Sources: Mozaffarian et al., Obesity 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12304835/; Look et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2025; WHO physical activity guidelines; US Physical Activity Guidelines.
plan.working_title: Protein on Tirzepatide: How Much and Why
plan.why:
Next unmade Lane A slot in the growth playbook. Practical tirzepatide long-forms earn about 2.4× the channel's median watch minutes, the topic rests on settled guideline sources that are easy to fact-check, Thanksgiving gives it a hook, and it doesn't overlap with today's Shorts. | fact-check: This is a good Lane A topic. It sits in an allowed pillar, nutrition guidance isn't drug dosing, and the population and DXA substudy figures match the channel's verified facts (Look et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2025). I checked the 2025 joint advisory (Mozaffarian et al., 'Nutritional priorities to support GLP-1 therapy for obesity', ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS, published together in Obesity, AJCN, Am J Lifestyle Med and Obesity Pillars; full text at PMC12304835). Four parts of the angle don't match what it actually says:
(1) The opening line says 'nutrition groups suggest putting a protein food at every meal'. The advisory never says 'every meal'. Its words are 'Protein-rich foods can be consumed first in a meal to increase the likelihood of sufficient consumption.'
(2) The higher range does exist, but it is hedged: 'Higher targets, such as 1.2–1.6 g/kg/day, have also been proposed.' The advisory also says it's unclear whether to use actual, adjusted/ideal body weight or fat-free mass, because actual weight 'can significantly overestimate protein requirements'. It offers an absolute target, '80–120 g/day ... may enhance adherence', and says prolonged intake at or above 2 g/kg/day 'should be avoided'. If the higher range is used, it must keep 'have been proposed' and the body-weight caveat.
(3) Chapter 5's supplement claim can't go out unsourced as 'our own summary'. It is a factual claim about the evidence, and the advisory actually says 'Some individuals can meet protein targets by supplementing with high-protein shakes, bars, and other fortified products.'
(4) 'Eating slowly' isn't in the advisory. Its GI advice is 'Smaller, more frequent meals and avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment can help alleviate symptoms.'
The advisory also says protein alone is 'likely inadequate' to keep muscle without resistance training. That supports chapter 6. On kidneys, it says people with or at risk of kidney problems should get advice on avoiding dehydration and have kidney function monitored. Two safety gaps: there's no eating-disorder caveat, and the Thanksgiving segment could slip into guilt framing. The title (40 characters, drug first, pays off), the 'Enough Protein?' thumbnail and the reaction layout are all fine.

package.description:
Quick answer: Adults in general are advised 0.8 g of protein per kg of body weight a day. During weight loss, about 1.2-1.6 g/kg has been proposed; a dietitian can set your number. Protein alone likely can't keep muscle without strength training. Common side effects include nausea, diarrhoea and constipation.

Not personal advice. Kidney disease, fluid limits, pregnancy or a history of disordered eating? Check with your clinician first. Don't stop or change your medicine on your own. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
1. Mozaffarian et al., Obesity 2025 (ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS advisory) - https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12304835/
2. Look et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2025 (SURMOUNT-1 body scans) - https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11965027/
3. WHO physical activity guidelines, 2020 - https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240015128
4. National Academies Dietary Reference Intakes (protein RDA), 2005 - https://doi.org/10.17226/10490

package.pinned_comment: In a SURMOUNT-1 body-scan substudy of adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes (124 on tirzepatide, all doses pooled, vs 36 on placebo, 72 weeks), about 75% of the weight lost on tirzepatide was fat and about 25% was lean mass, which isn't only muscle. A 2025 advisory says protein alone is likely not enough to keep muscle without strength training. Common side effects include nausea, diarrhoea and constipation. Save this for your next meal plan. Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

thumbnail.headline: PROTEIN + STRENGTH
thumbnail.psychology: Loss aversion, framed positively: viewers react more strongly to keeping muscle than to gaining something, and the SURMOUNT-1 scan data (about 25% of weight lost was lean mass) backs a calm, real reason to care.
thumbnail.emotion: Motivated: 'I want to hold on to what matters'

Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.") and the closing line: "There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description." No video title is spoken. Metadata: lane: A.

factcheck.summary:
The script passes, with five small wording fixes listed below. I checked the claims against the full text of the joint advisory (S1, Mozaffarian et al., Obesity 2025;33(8):1475–1503). It supports all of these:
- the 0.8 g/kg baseline, the proposed 1.2–1.6 g/kg target during weight loss, and the 80–120 g/day range "may enhance adherence"
- that it's unclear which body weight to use, and that using actual weight can overestimate need
- avoiding prolonged intake at or above 2 g/kg/day
- eating protein-rich foods first
- that protein alone is "likely inadequate" without resistance or strength training
- that shakes, bars and fortified products can help some people
- the advice on dehydration and kidney monitoring
- that the advisory recommends no product for keeping muscle

I confirmed the SURMOUNT-1 body-scan substudy (S2, Look et al., DOM 2025): 160 people had DXA scans over 72 weeks, and about 75% of the weight lost was fat and about 25% lean mass. The population is stated correctly (adults without diabetes). The worked maths is correct: 90 kg ≈ 198 lb, giving 72 g; 154 lb ≈ 70 kg, giving 56 g. I verified that the WHO 2020 and US Physical Activity Guidelines pages exist; their advice of muscle-strengthening on 2 or more days a week, working the major muscle groups, is standard. The script has the safety caveats it needs: kidneys, protein or fluid limits, pregnancy, disordered eating, a prescriber call if side effects make eating hard, the don't-stop-or-change line, and "Not personal advice" plus the prescriber line twice. Dana is clearly labelled as hypothetical. The open loop is paid off.

The fixes:
- s27: the quote card adds a word that isn't in the source.
- s52: the "avoid fatty foods" tip needs the advisory's scope (nausea, first few days).
- s22: "experts don't yet agree" is a little stronger than the source's "it is unclear".
- S2: the source link should be a canonical, non-redirecting URL.
- s55: the Thanksgiving reference doesn't suit an evergreen video for a mixed US/UK/CA/AU audience.

issues.claim: "Protein-rich foods can be consumed first in a meal to increase the likelihood of sufficient consumption."
issues.problem: This isn't verbatim. The advisory says "to increase likelihood of sufficient consumption", without "the". Only printed words may go inside quotes.
issues.fix: Narration and quote field: "Protein-rich foods can be consumed first in a meal to increase likelihood of sufficient consumption."

issues.claim: Smaller, more frequent meals and avoiding fatty foods, especially early on, can help.
issues.problem: The advisory gives this tip for nausea specifically, and the wording is "avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment". "Especially early on" stretches the timeframe, and the line drops what the tip is for.
issues.fix: Narration: "For nausea, the advisory says smaller, more frequent meals, and avoiding fatty or high-fibre foods in the first few days of treatment, can help." Second list item: "Easy on fatty or high-fibre foods, first few days".

issues.claim: But experts don't yet agree on which body weight to use.
issues.problem: The source says "it is unclear" whether to use actual, adjusted or ideal body weight, or fat-free mass. "Experts don't agree" frames it as a dispute and is a vague credit.
issues.fix: Narration: "But it's still unclear which body weight to use. Using your actual weight can overestimate what you need." On-screen: "Which weight? Still unclear".

issues.problem: The DOI redirects to a publisher landing domain. Our rules call for canonical URLs with no redirects.
issues.fix: Use https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11965027/ as the URL for S2.

issues.claim: Now, with Thanksgiving coming up, picture Dana at a full holiday table…
issues.problem: This isn't a factual error. But US Thanksgiving dates the video within weeks, and it doesn't fit the UK/AU audience or Canadians, whose Thanksgiving has already passed. That works against evergreen watch time.
issues.fix: Narration: "Now, picture Dana at a big celebration meal, with a much smaller appetite than she used to have." On-screen: "Big meal, smaller appetite". In s56, "Build the plate around turkey, or another protein you enjoy" can stay.

audio.soundNotes: Overall levels are close to target already (music ~-13.5 dB under voice, most SFX sitting in the -14 to -20 dB speech window); I left the auto-leveled music gain unchanged since it's already in the safe −12/−15 window and I don't want to risk re-triggering a masking hold. I pulled down 8 outlier cues that measured far too loud during speech (several blips/pops/hits sitting at -5 to -10 dB instead of -14 to -20), especially the dense 1-second cluster around t≈424-425 and the lone spike at t≈281.4 and t≈228. Everything else (transition whooshes in pauses at -6 to -12 dB, and the very quiet swells during dramatic one-liners) already matches the brief's intent and was left alone. Added five bespoke SFX to underline key story beats (appetite "food noise", the body-scan reveal, the kidney-caution pause, the checklist payoff, and the subscribe moment) without adding extra density to already-busy seconds.

issues: Subtext "when appetite drops" is tiny and likely unreadable at 168px phone-small size
"This" is vague with no food shown, which can feel like generic clickbait rather than a specific promise tied to the title's protein-amount question
Mascot emotion (plain happy) is less emotionally specific than the muscle-loss angle the video actually leads with
Two characters (before/after) rather than one, though the transformation framing is clear and intentional for this layout
Headline risks feeling contradictory next to a title about 'how much protein' — viewer may read it as the video dismissing protein rather than adding strength training, a mismatch risk
Negative/surprising framing is less aligned with brand's consistently positive tone than the other two options

thumbnail.reasoning: All three candidates are legible with large bold sans-serif caps and strong contrast, but #1 ("PROTECT YOUR MUSCLE") is the strongest match of packaging rules and content: it's a before-after layout (the channel's best-performing style, 6.5–7.3% CTR historically), has a single clean emotional arc (worried → confident), directly and honestly sets up the "why" behind the protein question (SURMOUNT-1 lean-mass data), and has no small or extraneous text that could get lost at phone size. #0 is appealing but its payoff-critical subtext ("when appetite drops") is likely unreadable at small sizes, and "EAT THIS FIRST" is a slightly generic curiosity hook that doesn't specifically connect to the muscle-preservation angle the script actually uses. #2 ("PROTEIN ISN'T ENOUGH") is honest per the script but creates a confusing signal against a title promising "how much and why" protein — a viewer could feel mildly misled expecting a protein-focused answer, and the negative framing cuts against the brand's consistently encouraging tone. #1 best balances strong emotional pull, perfect legibility, and honest alignment with the title's promise.

issues.claim: adults with obesity or overweight, without diabetes
issues.problem: The script says the trial enrolled adults with obesity, or with overweight plus a weight-related health condition. Dropping that condition makes the population slightly broader than the one the trial enrolled.
issues.fix: In a SURMOUNT-1 body-scan substudy of adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without diabetes (124 on tirzepatide, all doses pooled, vs 36 on placebo, 72 weeks),

issues.problem: Next to the title 'Protein on Tirzepatide', this could suggest protein alone protects muscle. The video says protein alone is likely not enough without strength training, and that no product is recommended for protecting muscle. The call to action isn't false, but it is a little stronger than the payoff.

issues.claim: Adults in general are advised 0.8 g of protein per kg of body weight a day.
issues.problem: The 0.8 g/kg figure is the National Academies RDA (verified source S5), but the description doesn't cite it. There is room for a 4th source.
issues.fix: Add a fourth source line: 4. National Academies Dietary Reference Intakes (protein RDA), 2005 - https://doi.org/10.17226/10490

hold_reason: Quality check: narration doesn't match script in 1 scene(s): expected "about" heard ""
approved_by: editor-in-chief (low risk): The only hold was a single dropped "about" in the narration. With final WER at 0.007, no numbers, decimals or drug names were garbled, so at worst one approximate figure sounds slightly more exact. The fact check and packaging check both passed with only minor fixes, the safety and prescriber lines are present, masking is 0.007 and the 9.7-minute length is within limits.
